meta: Aug 26, 2026  ·  expected vs actual, measured · the cap held
bluf: Before 1.2 started we wrote down the bet: $4,500, about 20 hours, wrong if the work left the 12 to 30 hour band. It did. The work ran roughly double the estimate, the $4,500 cap held, and this page shows the math: what blew the band, what you got for it, and what the receipt sets for 1.3. You pay the quote, never the overrun.

rows.title: Reliable delivery
rows.sub: A real chat becomes a complete, deduplicated, correctly-formatted CRM lead. The blank-email edge case that could update the wrong record is guarded and published; the one touched record is repaired; every test lead deleted and verified gone.

rows.title: Your baseline, pulled for the first time
rows.sub: 24 months: 942 leads, 4,238 opportunities. Headline finding: $43.7M of opportunities (48%) carry no lead source, so today no channel can prove its keep. The chatbot writes its source on every lead.

rows.title: Lead enrichment
rows.sub: Job title and industry auto-fill on every new lead. The one open question is whether your plan also returns business emails; ten minutes with your ZoomInfo contact closes it, either way, in writing.

rows.title: The four-hour rule
rows.sub: Your CRM does not stamp first-touch today, so the honest measure is a reminder email per lead plus an hourly sweep that flags anything sitting past four hours. One written “works” from you closes this line.

rows.title: The number stays inside the range you saw: $4,000
rows.sub: The overage was coordination, not build, so the fix is not a higher price. It is a different start: we close a short input list together in one sitting before the clock runs.

rows.title: The pre-start input list
rows.sub: Written sandbox approval · the ZoomInfo contact · the do-not-want lead list · the territory call with Bill. Each one arrived mid-phase in 1.2 and cost days; batched up front they cost an hour.
